pr_title: kubelet: Handle UID reuse in pod worker
pr_body:
If a pod is killed (no longer wanted) and then a subsequent create/add/update event is seen in the pod worker, assume that a pod UID was reused (as it could be in static pods) and have the next SyncKnownPods after the pod terminates remove the worker history so that the config loop can restart the static pod, as well as return to the caller the fact that this termination was not final.
    

1. If the pod worker sees updates KILL -> CREATE it sets a flag on the worker status restartRequested = true
2. When SyncKnownPods runs it reports any terminated worker with that flag as TemporarilyTerminatedWork
3. The pod housekeeping loop (which reconciles the pod worker with the config state) checks to see which pods were terminated but may need restart (TemporarilyTerminatedWork) during the sync, and starts them if they are not terminal (aka desired and admitted)

A pod that restarts this way will wait at most housekeeping loop period (2s) between being terminated and starting again.

/kind bug
/sig node

Fixes #104648

TODO:
* [ ] verifying this fixes the race

```release-note
Fix a 1.22 regression when a static pod file is deleted and recreated while using a fixed UID, the pod was not properly restarted.
```

```docs

```
pr_comments:
In theory this fixes the problem but you have to wait for a reconcile loop of ~90s.  A slightly more complex impl might queue the next pod.  I'll take a look at that.

Ideally SyncKnownPods would be able to restart workers, but SyncKnownPods doesn't get passed "the pods the pod worker should know about" today.  It needs to be "the admitted pods that should be running" which is a subset of what is in the pod manager.

Ok, after thinking through this some more I'm fairly convinced this is safe.  Builds on top of #104817 (which renames a bit of the admission logic):

1. If the pod worker sees updates `KILL -> CREATE` it sets a flag on the worker status `restartRequested = true`
2. When `SyncKnownPods` runs it reports any terminated worker with that flag as `TemporarilyTerminatedWork`
3. The pod housekeeping loop (which reconciles the pod worker with the config state) checks to see which pods were terminated but may need restart during the sync, and starts them if they are not terminal (aka desired and admitted)

A pod that restarts this way will wait at most `housekeeping loop period` (2s) between being terminated and starting again.

The containerStatus is going into Waiting state. We need to modify checkMirrorPodRunning to see if it's waiting and try again.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5d7cda1e6b438d9f4becd53c9a812f4f859c2724/test/e2e_node/mirror_pod_test.go#L251

/hold

to prevent accidental merging, want to give @Random-Liu a chance to review

Data in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104924 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104919 looks good, I'm comfortable with merging. Still working on adding one more test case for a manually set UID, we could merge that after.

/retest

issue_context.title: 1.22 regression: removing and recreating static pod manifest leaves pod in error state
issue_context.body:
#### What happened:

* Started a 1.22 cluster
* Added a static pod manifest
* Observed the pod run successfully
* Removed and recreated the pod manifest
* Observed the pod enter an error state and never restart successfully

#### What you expected to happen:

For the pod to be re-run successfully (as in previous releases)

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

```
# start a cluster
hack/local-up-cluster.sh

# create a static pod
echo '
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: mypod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $RANDOM; sleep 100000"]
' > mypod.yaml

sudo cp mypod.yaml /var/run/kubernetes/static-pods/

# wait until the pod is running
watch kubectl get pods -n default

# remove and recreate the static pod
sudo rm /var/run/kubernetes/static-pods/mypod.yaml
sudo cp mypod.yaml /var/run/kubernetes/static-pods/

# observe the pod remain in an error state
watch kubectl get pods -n default
```

#### Anything else we need to know?:

Bisected to 3eadd1a9ead7a009a9abfbd603a5efd0560473cc (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102344)

Broken in 1.22, works in 1.21 and previous versions.

/sig node
cc @smarterclayton @bobbypage @rphillips
comments: I also verified the pending PR fixing the 1.22 [pod admission regression](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104560) (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104611) does not fix this issue

this seems likely to be caused by the pod cleanup being keyed by uid and not handling an overlapping delete operation and recreate operation for a pod with the same uid

the calculated uid for static pods consists of:
* node name
* file name
* pod content

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/edb0a72cff0e43bab72a02cada8486d562ee1cd5/pkg/kubelet/config/common.go#L57-L70

Removing and then replacing the manifest resulted in a pod with an identical computed uid.

Changing any of the manifest inputs to the pod uid calculation resulted in the second pod starting successfully:
* removing the first manifest and creating an identical manifest with a different filename
* removing the first manifest and creating a manifest with the same name with a slightly different pod (e.g. a random annotation inserted)

Also, waiting for the pod deletion to complete (typically takes a few seconds), then readding the manifest resulting in an identical pod UID worked.

I can imagine schemes for including a generation var for static manifest files, where every time the kubelet observes a deletion of a manifest file, it bumps the generation of that file, and generations above 0 are included in the computed pod uid.

Is it important for the kubelet's calculated uid for a static pod to remain stable over kubelet restarts (e.g. does it get baked into a persistent attribute in the CRI and compared by the kubelet in a way that a kubelet restart that changed the computed uid would restart the container)?
/assign @smarterclayton @rphillips

I tested https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104031 and it does not fix this issue.

How about including file modification time when calculating the static pod's uid.

The rough structure you described is similar to #104847, except we need to do this for non static pods as well.  There are a couple of problems related to a change like this though because the rest of the Kubelet ONLY references a pod by UID.  So if you were to rapidly delete a pod and create a new one with the same UID AND completely change volumes or devices, it's very likely that other parts of the Kubelet could perform some of their cleanup or tear down logic inconsistently.  I *think* volumes are correct (although that's only if setup and teardown are happening in serial), but I haven't reviewed the others.  Just waiting some unit of time isn't enough - we need to either guarantee those loops are safe for two separate pod definitions with the same UID to be passed to them in quick succession (better testing + review) or we need to add a construct that ensures that those loops don't think the pod is the same (such as a second UID in the kubelet or a generation or something).

The real tension here is that reusing a UID for a completely different instance of a pod (like static pods allow) is not desirable, because UID is supposed to represent an "instance of a pod" and pods provide certain one way guarantees around lifecycle (once a pod is failed, it stays that way forever).  The behavior of static pods shouldn't be modelled like a pod that lives forever, it should be modelled using a controller that stamps out new desired pods (each with their own UID).  However, that's a behavior change, and it's of course possible (but incredibly unlikely) for a duplicate UID to be generated on the apiserver, so the easiest path probably is just "prevent uid reuse from being inconsistent".

In which case, the design of what we're trying to do in Kubelet is:

1. Ensure that the pod worker runs at most one  pod definition with a given uid at a time
2. Ensure that when a pod with a given UID exits, if the pod is still desired with that UID, the new one is started in the pod worker

That's hard to do outside the pod worker today because the loop that drives pod worker is edge driven (change to pod config), not level driven.  We'd need to fix the loop from pod config to pod worker to reconcile the desired state against the actual state, and the kubelet doesn't directly track desired state (because admission decisions aren't recorded in a single list).  But we can't do it from within the pod worker, because we have no idea when the pod worker receives the sequence `STOP(uid=1) -> CREATE(uid=1) -> STOP(uid=1)` whether the second stop cancels the `CREATE` or is simply shortening the first `STOP`.

Probably having pod housekeeping filter the list of desired pods and then have it start any pod that is still desired but is terminated in the Kubelet is the right fix, but I need to think through the tradeoffs some more.  The biggest tradeoff is pod housekeeping happens on a schedule, which means suddenly static pods sharing the same UID that are deleted and recreated suddenly take longer to restart (which I guess is good because it gently penalizes users for using static pod UIDs and doing delete/recreate).

Elaborating on this a little bit... Right now, we see the following behaviour when a node reboots:

- Static pods terminate, node shuts down
- Node starts up, kubelet does its reconciliation loop
- Static pods are launched prior to API server sync and enter pending state, if the container runtime does not retain information on the previous static pod status [true on OpenShift because we call cri-o wipe, but this could also happen on manual wipe or during disaster recovery]
- New static pods use the same UID as the manifests are unchanged
- Kubelet eventually syncs with API server. Mirror pod with the same UID used to be running, but if it doesn't launch fast enough, kubelet will sync a new Pending status
- Pod illegally transitions back from Running->Pending

So IMO the reuse of the UID is a bit of a hack that breaks core assumptions of the kubelet.

> Pod illegally transitions back from Running->Pending

Turns out this actually is not an illegal transition (which I realized during dealing with soft admission).  A pod that fails soft admission post start is put back into pending because it's not actually running and the kubelet has decided to hold it.  It's strictly better for the kubelet to communicate this because the alternative is a user has no idea that the pod wouldn't be running.  So I think going forward Running -> Pending is a bug when  we're losing state (i.e. restart with wipe) or when we know there is a concrete transition (soft admitted to soft not-admitted)
